newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan views Dalai Lama as a local citizen.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan views Dalai Lama as a local citizen.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday said Tibet's exiled leader, the Dalai Lama, would be welcomed in Taiwan this week as a local citizen -- something likely to irk arch rival China as well as the Buddhist god-king himself.
"Tibet is a part of the Republic of China and the Dalai Lama is a republic national," said Chang King-yuh, head of the cabinet's policy-making Mainland Affairs Council.
"He will not be treated as a state guest during his Taiwan trip," Chang said.
Taiwan analysts said Chang seemed to be trying to play down the political tone of the Dalai Lama's visit -- but was likely to anger arch rival China and even the Tibetan monk.
Tibetan Buddhism's top cleric has never acknowledged being a subject of the exiled Republic of China on Taiwan or the communist People's Republic of China that took power in 1949.
Beijing was likely to bristle over Chang's characterisation of the Dalai Lama as a national of the Nationalist Republic of China, whose civil war defeat came by the communists' hand.
Beijing characterises the 1989 Nobel peace laureate as a "splittist" seeking Tibet's independence from China.
His scheduled March 22-27 Taiwan visit has already angered China, even more so after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui said last week he hoped to meet the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader.

Beijing, which assails Lee as a "schemer" who secretly plots Taiwan's formal independence from China, has warned Taiwan not to admit the Dalai Lama so as not to harm China's reunification and ethnic unity.
Chang said the Dalai Lama's trip was a religious rather than political one, noting that the Dalai Lama's government in exile no longer advocated a unified church-state as it once did.
"Besides, from our point of view, Tibet has never become independent," Chang told parliament, expressing a view identical to that held by rival China.
Beijing has alleged that the Dalai Lama's Taiwan visit has political motives.
Taiwan's parliament has invited the Dalai Lama to address the body.

Advocates of Taiwan's independence from China have said they would seek to meet the Dalai Lama during his visit. The radical Taiwan Independence Party vowed to send hundreds of supporters to welcome the exiled leader at the airport.
The Dalai Lama has accused Beijing of waging "cultural genocide" in Tibet and called for talks with China's leaders to secure political autonomy for the vast Himalayan region.
The cleric fled Tibet after a failed anti-Chinese uprising in 1959 and has lived in exile in India ever since.
